idiom_name: casbin-rs Enforcer (model.conf + policy.csv) shared behind Arc<RwLock<>> from an actix-web/axum guard; an enum role + BTreeSet<Permission> for small systems
implementation_notes: The Rust realization of the table model is casbin-rs: Enforcer::new("model.conf", "policy.csv").await (or an adapter over a database), then e.enforce((sub, obj, act))? with a model whose [role_definition] g = _, _ builds the role links; the RBAC API adds and removes roles/permissions at runtime. Because the Enforcer is not thread-safe, a web server holds one behind Arc<RwLock<Enforcer>> (or the actor pattern) and the framework's guard - an actix-web middleware (actix-casbin) or an axum layer - calls enforce and rejects with 403 on false. Where the dependency is unwanted, the honest hand-rolled form is an enum Role paired with a BTreeSet<Permission> per role plus a static hierarchy map closed at startup; the decision is a set lookup, and enum roles make the vocabulary exhaustive and typo-proof. Either way the subject comes from the verified principal (see authenticator), the guard is the single mediation point, and every error path denies.
pitfalls: Enforcer is not Sync; sharing it without Arc<RwLock<Enforcer>> (or the actor pattern) does not compile, and holding the write lock across an .await serializes the request path.
unwrap() on enforce turns an evaluation error into a panic; map the error to deny and keep serving.
Rebuilding the enforcer per request reloads the policy from disk; keep one instance and reload explicitly on a watcher.
Taking the subject or its roles from request headers or a deserialized body lets a caller widen its own permissions; use the authenticated principal.
A hand-rolled hierarchy must be cycle-free and closed once at startup; walking it per request risks unbounded recursion and allocation.
